distillation_scope.scope_note: A first-layer disease manifold for infected pleural-space pus or culture/Gram-positive pleural infection, regardless of parapneumonic, aspiration, post-procedure, fistulous, hematogenous, or subdiaphragmatic route.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Microbial entry into the pleural space
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, or mixed flora reach the pleural cavity from adjacent pneumonia or lung abscess, aspiration-related infection, thoracic surgery or trauma, esophageal or bronchopleural fistula, hematogenous seeding, or subdiaphragmatic infection.
Ongoing replication of organisms in pleural fluid and fibrin septa, often with reduced antibiotic penetration until pus is drained and active coverage is established.
Intense neutrophil influx, bacterial products, cellular debris, and proteases convert exudative pleural fluid into turbid or frank purulent fluid with high cell count and high LDH.
Neutrophil and bacterial metabolism plus impaired pleural transport drive low pleural pH, low glucose, high LDH, and urgent drainage physiology.
Fibrin deposition and impaired pleural fluid turnover produce septations, locules, split pleura enhancement, inadequate tube drainage, and need for intrapleural enzyme therapy or surgery.
Pleural pus compresses lung, adjacent pneumonia impairs ventilation-perfusion matching, and pleuritic splinting worsens atelectasis, producing dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia.
Pleural infection triggers IL-1, IL-6, TNF, acute phase reactants, fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia, hypotension, lactate rise, organ dysfunction, and sepsis mortality risk.

Inadequate drainage, thick pus, malpositioned tube, unrecognized locules, ongoing bronchopleural or transdiaphragmatic source, or inactive antibiotics sustain fever, CRP elevation, bacteremia, trapped lung, and death risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Organizing pleural peel and trapped lung
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Fibroblast invasion and pleural thickening organize the infected space, causing restricted lung re-expansion, chronic symptoms, recurrent infection, and surgical decortication need.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Entry of viable organisms into the pleural cavity initiates sustained infected pleural fluid.
Pleural organisms and bacterial products recruit neutrophils and create pus.
Neutrophil metabolism and bacterial glycolysis lower pleural pH and glucose.
Inflamed pleura deposits fibrin and partitions the infected collection.
Septations and thick pus make single-catheter drainage less complete.
Persistent fibrinopurulent pleuritis evolves into organizing peel and trapped lung.
Active pleural infection commonly causes fever, though frailty or immunosuppression can blunt it.
Fever, pain, hypoxemia, and sepsis drive tachycardia.
Compression, pneumonia, and pleuritic splinting increase ventilatory drive.
Atelectasis and shunt lower oxygen saturation.
Neutrophilic bacterial infection usually raises WBC unless host response is impaired.
IL-6 acute phase response raises CRP, often markedly in empyema.
Bacterial pleural infection and sepsis can raise procalcitonin, especially with invasive organisms.
Shock and tissue hypoperfusion raise lactate.
Purulence is the macroscopic expression of neutrophilic pleural suppuration.
Pleural WBC rises with neutrophil influx.
Acute bacterial empyema is typically neutrophil predominant.
Cell lysis and inflammation markedly increase pleural LDH.
Pleural pH below 7.2 identifies complicated infection physiology.
Pleural glucose falls with microbial and leukocyte metabolism.
Higher burden increases direct smear yield.
Viable pleural organisms determine culture yield, modified by pre-treatment antibiotics and anaerobic handling.
Fibrin septation produces loculated pleural collections.
Inflamed enhancing visceral and parietal pleura produce the split pleura sign.
Gas-forming organisms, bronchopleural fistula, or introduced air can produce pleural air-fluid level.
Pleural fluid and compressed lung reduce breath sounds.
Pleural fluid creates stony dullness or dullness to percussion.
Organizing peel prevents re-expansion after drainage.
Undrained pleural sepsis increases respiratory failure, shock, and death.
Septic shock and organ dysfunction are central causes of death in pleural infection.
Large effusion, consolidation, and atelectasis can require oxygen escalation or ventilation.
Pleural infection can progress to septic shock.
Residual undrained space and persistent fistula predispose to chronic or recurrent empyema.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Fever is common but may be absent in frailty, chronic disease, or partial antibiotic treatment.
History of fever, chills, or rigors can be more sensitive than a single measured temperature.
Inflamed parietal pleura causes sharp pain worsened by inspiration or cough; can mimic pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, or referred abdominal pain.
Generic chest or hypochondrial pain from pleural irritation, chest tube site, or adjacent pneumonia.
Cough reflects adjacent pneumonia, aspiration, bronchopleural fistula, or lung compression; may be absent in extrapulmonary empyema.
Copious or foul sputum supports anaerobic aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess, or bronchopleural communication.
Dyspnea rises with large effusion, pneumonia, atelectasis, hypoxemia, or sepsis.
Subacute empyema can present with malaise, anorexia, and prolonged inflammatory symptoms.
Chronic anaerobic, tuberculosis-associated, malignancy-associated, or fistulous empyema may cause weight loss.
Tachypnea tracks respiratory compromise and sepsis.
Tachycardia reflects fever, pain, hypoxemia, and septic physiology.
Hypotension appears with septic shock; hypertension may coexist as background.
Low MAP marks septic shock and increases mortality hazard.
May be normal in localized empyema or low with large effusion, pneumonia, atelectasis, or ARDS.
Diminished breath sounds over the affected hemithorax reflect pleural fluid and atelectasis.
Dullness or stony dullness supports a pleural fluid collection.
Adjacent pneumonia or atelectasis can produce crackles; empyema itself can have reduced sounds instead.
Leukocytosis is common; extreme values can occur with severe pleural infection or sepsis.
Bacterial empyema usually shows peripheral neutrophilia.
Platelets may be normal, reactive high in inflammation, or low in sepsis, liver disease, HIV, or drug toxicity.
CRP is often markedly elevated and should fall after active antibiotics plus drainage.
May rise with bacterial pleural infection and sepsis but can be modest in localized or chronic disease.
Elevated lactate reflects sepsis-induced hypoperfusion rather than empyema morphology itself.
Hypoalbuminemia reflects inflammation, frailty, liver disease, or chronic illness and worsens outcomes.
A pleural fluid collection is necessary but not sufficient for empyema.
Ranges from small loculated fluid to near hemithorax opacification.
Septated or loculated collection on ultrasound or CT is a key empyema morphology.
Enhancing thickened visceral and parietal pleura on contrast CT helps distinguish empyema from lung abscess or simple effusion.
Gas in the pleural collection suggests bronchopleural fistula, gas-forming organisms, esophageal/abdominal source, or prior pleural instrumentation.
Pleural thickening appears in established infection and organizing empyema; malignancy and TB remain important mimics.
Drainable pus volume varies widely and is often estimated on CT or by drainage output.
Adjacent pneumonia is common but not required for post-procedure, fistulous, or subdiaphragmatic empyema.
Consolidation marks parapneumonic empyema or compressive adjacent lung change.
Compressive or post-obstructive atelectasis is common with large empyema.
Macroscopic pus at thoracentesis or drainage is diagnostic of empyema.

axes.axis_name: Pleural fluid white blood cell count
axes.clinical_interpretation: Complicated pleural infection is usually highly cellular, but very viscous pus may be hard to count.
Most bacterial empyemas are neutrophil-predominant; TB or chronic inflammatory mimics can be lymphocyte-predominant.
Low pleural pH is a drainage criterion and severity marker.
Low pleural glucose supports complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, but rheumatoid and malignant effusions can also be low.
LDH usually becomes very high in complicated infection because of cell lysis and inflammation.
Empyema is exudative; protein helps classify fluid but is less specific than pus, pH, glucose, and microbiology.
Positive Gram stain establishes infected pleural fluid, but sensitivity is limited after antibiotics or with anaerobes.
Culture yield depends on organism burden, prior antibiotics, anaerobic transport, and sampling quality.
Raised by aspiration, poor dentition, foul sputum, lung abscess, chronic course, and polymicrobial infection.
Raised by healthcare exposure, influenza, IV drug use, thoracic procedures, bacteremia, or necrotizing pneumonia.
Streptococci, including anginosus group and pneumococcus, are common causes of community-acquired pleural infection.
Raised by hospital exposure, aspiration, Enterobacterales, urologic or abdominal sources, and immunocompromise.
Raised by TB exposure, prior TB cavity, pleural instrumentation, immunosuppression, chronic course, or fungal epidemiology.
Bacteremia occurs in a subset and raises sepsis and metastatic infection risk.
Probability that the current regimen covers the actual organism mix at adequate pleural and systemic exposure.
Frank pus, positive Gram/culture, low pH/glucose, loculation, large collection, or clinical nonresponse create source-control need.
Adequacy rises after complete drainage, lung re-expansion, defervescence, and falling inflammatory markers.
Tube output, imaging resolution, and lung re-expansion describe the pleural source-control component.
Need rises when residual loculated fluid persists after catheter drainage.
Need rises with failed tube drainage/fibrinolytics, organizing peel, trapped lung, or chronic calcified empyema.
Subdiaphragmatic abscess, esophageal perforation, perinephric infection, hepatic abscess, trauma, or surgery can seed the pleura.
Risk rises with necrotizing pneumonia, trauma, surgery, chronic empyema, or pleural air-fluid level.
Organized pleural peel prevents lung expansion and can require decortication.
Hazard rises with hypoxemia, bilateral disease, large effusion, pneumonia, ARDS, or sepsis.
Severe pneumonia, sepsis, and aspiration-associated empyema can progress to ARDS.
Shock hazard rises with bacteremia, delayed drainage, inactive antibiotics, frailty, and gram-negative or staphylococcal disease.
AKI hazard tracks sepsis, nephrotoxic antibiotics, contrast, and baseline CKD.
Chest tube, fibrinolytics, surgery, thrombocytopenia, anticoagulation, or coagulopathy raise bleeding risk.
Residual space, trapped lung, fistula, persistent source, or incomplete therapy raises recurrence/chronicity.
Lifespan hazard emerges from septic shock, respiratory failure, frailty, comorbidity, delayed active antibiotics, and incomplete source control.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Larger infected effusions have more surface for fibrin partitioning and locule formation.
Loculated collections are less likely to resolve with antibiotics alone.
Lower pH indicates complicated pleural infection physiology and drainage need.
Low glucose tracks infected, metabolically active pleural fluid.
Adequate drainage and active therapy should lower CRP; persistent elevation suggests missed locules or source.
Mortality falls when pleural infection source control is achieved.
Active antibiotics lower microbial burden but cannot replace drainage for frank pus.
Large pleural collections compress lung and worsen oxygenation.
Large effusions and reduced breath sounds co-vary on physical examination.
Pleural gas without recent instrumentation raises concern for bronchopleural communication or gas-forming infection.
Thickened organizing pleura can mature into trapped lung.
Trapped lung makes decortication more likely when clinically meaningful.
Septic shock strongly increases short-term death hazard.
Respiratory failure is a major pathway to death in pleural infection.
Bleeding risk from drainage, fibrinolytics, or surgery can affect outcomes in anticoagulated or coagulopathic patients.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Inactive empiric coverage cannot reduce the true pleural microbial burden.
Antibiotics alone underperform when frank pus or loculations need drainage.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad-spectrum and prolonged antibiotic exposure can cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea, including C. difficile risk context.

treatments.context_specific_role: Covers common community pleural pathogens including streptococci and anaerobes; narrow once pleural and blood culture data clarify susceptibility.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: MRSA-active therapy matters when healthcare, post-influenza, procedure, or bacteremic contexts raise MRSA probability.
Antipseudomonal or Enterobacterales-active coverage matters when hospital, aspiration, urologic, or abdominal source is plausible.

side_effects.interpretation: Vancomycin and antipseudomonal beta-lactams can increase AKI risk in vulnerable patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broadens empiric coverage for hospital-acquired, post-procedural, severe, or resistant-risk pleural infection until microbiology supports de-escalation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Aspiration, foul sputum, poor dentition, lung abscess, or polymicrobial culture make anaerobic coverage valuable.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adds or preserves anaerobic activity when the source or smell/course suggests anaerobes even if cultures are negative.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ultrasound guidance and careful site selection matter most for small or loculated effusions.

side_effects.interpretation: Small bleeding risk, higher with coagulopathy or anticoagulation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Obtains pH, glucose, LDH, cell count, Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic culture, and cytology/AFB/fungal studies when context supports them.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage is the central intervention for frank empyema.
A single tube may not drain all locules without enzyme therapy or surgery.

side_effects.interpretation: Bleeding, pain, pneumothorax, or organ injury risk depends on anatomy and coagulation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Evacuates pus and enables lung re-expansion; imaging guidance matters for loculated collections.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: tPA/DNase targets fibrin septation and viscous DNA-rich pus.
Bleeding risk changes the expected value of fibrinolysis.

side_effects.interpretation: Intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy can cause pleural bleeding, especially with anticoagulation or coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Improves drainage when residual loculated empyema persists despite a drain.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Surgery is most valuable when drainage/enzyme therapy cannot clear locules or peel.
Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and frailty increase procedural risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Surgical bleeding risk depends on coagulopathy, pleural vascularity, and adhesions.

treatments.context_specific_role: Clears loculated or organized empyema when catheter drainage and enzyme therapy are inadequate or not feasible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: A perinephric, hepatic, esophageal, chest wall, or post-surgical source must be addressed when it continues to seed the pleura.

side_effects.interpretation: Risk depends on the drained source and approach.

treatments.context_specific_role: Drain or repair abdominal, renal, esophageal, chest wall, airway, or foreign-body source when pleural infection is not purely parapneumonic.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large shunt/compression may blunt oxygen response until drainage.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supports oxygenation while antibiotics and source control treat the underlying pleural process.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic support matters when shock physiology is present.

side_effects.interpretation: Excess crystalloid can worsen pulmonary edema or oxygenation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Stabilizes septic shock while definitive antibiotic and drainage effects accumulate.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises parapneumonic pleural-space inoculation and pulmonary-source probability.
Raises anaerobic and polymicrobial pleural infection, foul sputum, lung abscess, and prolonged course.
Raises incidence, atypical presentation, delayed diagnosis, source-control risk, and mortality.
Raises severe infection, gram-negative infection, fungal risk in selected contexts, source-control failure, and mortality.
Broadens microbiology, blunts fever or leukocytosis, raises tuberculosis/fungal probability, and increases mortality.
Raises pneumonia, gram-negative colonization, hypoxemia, poor reserve, and chronicity.
Raises direct pleural inoculation, staphylococcal and gram-negative organisms, pleural air, bronchopleural fistula, and chronic empyema.
Raises pleural contamination, anaerobes, pleural gas, source-control failure, and mortality unless repaired or drained.
Raises gram-negative and anaerobic empyema from hepatic, perinephric, psoas, biliary, bowel, pancreatic, or diaphragmatic-defect spread.
Raises MRSA, Pseudomonas, resistant Enterobacterales, inactive initial therapy, and toxicity from broader regimens.
Raises tuberculosis pleural infection/empyema probability and chronicity; TB pleuritis remains a close mimic when pus or bacterial evidence is absent.
Sustains microbial burden, loculation, organizing peel, sepsis, and mortality.

supportive_care: Use contrast chest CT and thoracic ultrasound to define pleural size, septations, split pleura sign, drainable locules, adjacent consolidation, lung abscess, pleural gas, and trapped lung.
Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible; start active systemic antibiotics promptly when pleural infection or sepsis is suspected.

Perform diagnostic thoracentesis for suspected pleural infection unless immediate drainage is already indicated; send pH in heparinized blood-gas syringe, glucose, LDH, protein, cell count/differential, Gram stain, aerobic and anaerobic cultures, and targeted AFB/fungal/cytology tests when context supports them.
Do not rely on a negative pleural culture to exclude empyema when antibiotics, anaerobic pathogens, or poor sample handling reduce yield.
Drain frank pus, positive Gram stain/culture, pleural pH below 7.2, very low glucose, large symptomatic collection, loculated collection, or persistent sepsis.
Use image-guided tube or pigtail placement aimed at the dominant locule; reassess tube position and output early.
Trend temperature, heart rate, respiratory status, oxygen requirement, WBC, CRP, procalcitonin when available, lactate, kidney function, and drainage output.
Re-image within 24-72 hours if fever, pain, hypoxemia, leukocytosis, CRP, or sepsis persists after antibiotics and drainage.
Consider intrapleural tPA/DNase for residual loculated pleural infection when bleeding risk is acceptable.
Escalate to VATS debridement or decortication when catheter drainage and enzyme therapy fail, when organized peel causes trapped lung, or when chronic empyema persists.

Search for and control non-pulmonary sources when microbiology, imaging, or course suggests subdiaphragmatic abscess, renal infection, esophageal perforation, chest wall infection, foreign body, trauma, or post-surgical source.
Adjust antibiotic regimen to local resistance, healthcare exposure, aspiration/anaerobic risk, renal function, hepatic function, allergy, pregnancy, and pleural/blood culture susceptibility.
Use oxygen, ventilatory support, analgesia, mobilization, nutrition, DVT prophylaxis, glycemic control, renal dosing, and sepsis resuscitation according to physiologic need.

Arrange follow-up imaging and clinical review to document resolution, detect trapped lung or recurrence, and evaluate underlying malignancy, TB, bronchial obstruction, aspiration risk, or immunodeficiency when the cause is not obvious.
